This report demonstrates that in a case of intractability to
fosphenytoin treatment in status epilepticus, besides an underly-
ing cause, a failure to achieve therapeutic levels of phenytoin
must be considered. Although the nature of this phenomenon is
uncertain, switching to conventional phenytoin or other antiepi-
leptic drugs should be considered.

Paraneoplastic stiff-person syndrome:
No tumor progression over 5 years
K. Schmierer, MD; P. Grosse, MD; P. De Camilli, MD;
M. Solimena, MD, PhD; S. Floyd, MD; and R. Zschenderlein, MD
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder characterized by
progressive stiffness of predominantly axial and proximal limb
muscles, and painful spasms that are often precipitated by startle,
emotional, and tactile stimuli.
1 Evidence for an autoimmune
pathogenesis has been derived from the detection of autoantibod-
ies against glutamic acid decarboxylase in serum and CSF in up to
90% of SPS cases.
2,3 In occasional cases, SPS is considered to be of
paraneoplastic origin, with amphiphysin being presumably the
most common autoantigen.
4,5
Case report. Three years ago, we reported a 53-year old woman
with atypical SPS who presented with stiffness predominantly of
her right upper limb and trunk.
6 This case was unusual for MRI
findings of an intramedullary hyperintense lesion corresponding
to the site of the clinical symptoms. The neurologic symptoms of
the patient improved strikingly after initial treatment with IV
methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide. After 3 years of im-
munosuppressive treatment, she showed no clinical signs of SPS
while taking methylprednisolone 6 mg/day by mouth.
Despite the initial presence of amphiphysin-autoantibodies in

the serum and CSF of the patient, we failed to detect a malig-
nancy. We therefore concluded that the patient’s SPS was not
paraneoplastic, particularly because amphiphysin-autoantibodies
were negative after immunosuppressive treatment. However,
more than 5 years after SPS onset, clinical and radiologic (mam-
mography, ultrasound, MRI) observation of a nonpalpable, small
nodule (1.5 /H110031.5 cm) in the right breast has led us to reconsider
this conclusion.
MRI-guided biopsy of the nodule revealed no malignancy at 3.5
years after onset of SPS. Yet, 1.5 years after that, the patient first
reported discomfort in her right breast, although no changes in
size or morphology suggesting malignancy could be detected by
imaging. Open surgery, however, unveiled an infiltrating ductal
carcinoma of the breast (size: 1.7 /H110031.2 /H110031 cm), which was
classified as moderately differentiated (G2; pT1c according to
UICC TNM classification). The tissue showed a strong expression
of amphiphysin at a molecular weight of 108 kD, as detected by
Western blot.
5 All of the 18 resected axillary lymph nodes were
tumor free and there was no evidence of metastatic spread. The
patient was therefore treated with tamoxifen and focal
radiotherapy.
Discussion. In view of these findings, it seems warranted to
reclassify this case of SPS with amphiphysin-autoantibodies as
being of paraneoplastic origin. Its most interesting feature is the
very limited progression of the cancer over 5 years, despite the
tumor being only moderately differentiated. A likely explanation
for the benign course is that the autoimmune response causing
SPS also allowed the rejection of the cancer.
7

Sporadic CJD clinically mimicking variant
CJD with bilateral increased signal in the
pulvinar
S. Haïk, MD; J.P. Brandel, MD, PhD; C. Oppenheim, MD;
V. Sazdovitch, MD; D. Dormont, MD; J.J. Hauw, MD; and
C. Marsault, MD
The premortem diagnosis of probable new-variant Creutzfeldt –
Jakob disease (vCJD) may have important implications in terms
of public health. Recently, a bilaterally increased pulvinar signal
on T2-weighted MRI has been described in patients with vCJD.
1,2
The presence of a pulvinar high signal is necessary to classify a
suspect case as probable vCJD according to the recently proposed
diagnostic criteria, the estimated specificity of which is 100%.
3 We
report routine MRI and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) fea-
tures in a neuropathologically confirmed case of sporadic CJD,
which exhibits a bilateral increased signal in the pulvinar and a
clinical phenotype of vCJD.
Case report. A 55-year-old woman with no history of iatrogenic
exposure to CJD was referred to a neurologic center for behavioral
148 NEUROLOGY 58 January (1 of 2) 2002

disorders. She acted aggressively toward her coworkers and fam-
ily and quickly developed jealous delusions, dyscalculia, and mem-
ory impairments. Over the next year, her psychiatric signs
worsened, and visual hallucinations and frontal lobe symptoms
presented. Apraxia, spatial orientation anomalies, and parkinson-
ism occurred and the patient progressively developed cerebellar
ataxia and myoclonus. Over the next 6 months, extrapyramidal
rigidity, myoclonus, cognitive impairment, and hallucinations
worsened. Fluent jargon aphasia, pyramidal signs, and terminal
akinetic mutism occurred, and the patient died 21 months after
the inaugural symptoms.
Standard CSF examination and brain CT results were normal.
Typical periodic sharp-wave complexes were not found on re-
peated EEG. Detection of the 14-3-3 protein in the CSF by West-
ern blot was positive. A history of tonsillectomy precluded tonsil
biopsy.
MRI of the brain performed with a 1.5-T MRI unit (GE Signa
Horizon Echospeed, Milwaukee, WI) 6 months before death
showed several abnormalities (figure). A moderately increased sig-
nal of the pulvinar on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR)
images was detected in association with hyperintensity of the
dorsomedial nucleus of the thalamus, leading to the typical “hock-
ey stick aspect.” There was high signal in the striatum, which
involved the putamen and the caudate nucleus in contrast to a
strikingly normal aspect of the pallidum. Two fine, hyperintense
bands were also present, probably corresponding to the claustrum
and the insular cortex. A diffuse high signal was also identified in
the isocortex. Abnormal signal areas seen on FLAIR corresponded
to hyperintense areas on DWI.
The patient’s family gave informed consent for the genetic and
postmortem studies. Genotyping the human prion protein gene
(PRNP) revealed methionine/valine heterozygosity at codon 129.
The neuropathologic study showed severe lesions of the basal gan-
glia, the cerebellum, and the isocortex, in which numerous Kuru-
like amyloid plaques were present. Intense lesions were found in
the pulvinar and the dorsomedial nucleus of the thalamus. No
florid plaques were detected despite careful investigation. In
Western blot, a type 2 protease resistant prion protein (PrPsc) was
found.
4 The final diagnosis was sporadic CJD.
Discussion. Because vCJD, along with other human prion dis-
eases, can only be diagnosed through neuropathologic examina-
tion,
5,6 the need for an accurate noninvasive diagnostic test is
particularly important. Recently, diagnostic criteria for vCJD
have been proposed. According to these criteria, the presence of a
bilateral pulvinar high signal on MRI scanning is a necessary
condition to classify a suspected case as a probable vCJD and is
considered the most discriminating component.
3 The estimated
specificity of these diagnostic criteria is 100%. MRI of the sporadic
CJD case reported here showed an obvious bilateral increased
signal in the pulvinar on FLAIR images and DWI. Therefore,
considering the clinical history and the duration of the disease,
the case could be falsely classified as probable vCJD according to
the proposed diagnostic criteria.
3 However, in this case and on a
highly sensitive T2-weighted sequence (FLAIR), signal changes
were more prominent in the striatum than in the thalamus. This
MRI pattern has been reported in 7% of sporadic CJD cases,
7 but
does not constitute the pulvinar sign, which was recently de-

scribed in vCJD as bilateral pulvinar high signal relative to all
other basal ganglia.
1
We conclude that even in a case with a confusing clinical
course and a long duration of disease, which exhibits a pulvinar
high signal with a “hockey stick aspect” on MRI and prominent
lesions in the posterior thalamus at autopsy, the pulvinar sign
may not be found on highly sensitive sequences. Therefore, it is a
useful discriminating sign between vCJD and atypical sporadic
CJD. The presence of the pulvinar sign (defined as a bilateral
high-signal intensity greater than all other basal ganglia) should
be included in the diagnostic criteria for probable vCJD, rather
than a bilateral pulvinar high signal.
